title: Index types and how to pick
scopeHtml: Scope: B-tree, composite, covering, partial, hash, inverted and geo indexes, and how to choose and verify them.

notes.title: What an index is and what it costs
notes.html:
An index is an extra, sorted (or hashed) structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. The table is the book; the index is the back-of-book index mapping a term to page numbers.

Benefit: a lookup in a 100M-row table drops from reading everything (tens of seconds) to reading a handful of pages (around a millisecond). Cost: every insert, update of an indexed column and delete must also update every index on the table, and each index takes disk and RAM.

Worked example. Table orders, 100M rows, 200 B each = 20 GB. An index on customer_id (8 B key + 6 B pointer, about 20 B per entry with overhead) is about 2 GB. Writing a new order now touches the table plus each index: with 5 indexes, one insert is about 6 page modifications, which is why write throughput drops as indexes pile up.

Industry examples. Instagram and Shopify engineering posts repeatedly cite "missing index" as the cause of the worst slow-query incidents; GitHub uses extensive indexes plus strict query review on MySQL.

Everyday analogy. A textbook index: very fast to look something up, but whenever an author edits a chapter, someone must also update the index.

Common interview traps.

  • "Add an index" with no thought for write cost and memory.
  • Forgetting that low-selectivity columns (a boolean) rarely benefit from a plain index.
  • Assuming an index is always used; the planner may prefer a scan if it returns a large fraction of the table.

notes.title: B-tree indexes: the default
notes.html:
The default index in Postgres, MySQL and most databases is a B-tree (usually B+tree). It keeps keys sorted, so it supports equality (=), range (<, >, BETWEEN), ORDER BY, prefix LIKE 'abc%' (with the right collation), and MIN/MAX. Height is usually 3 to 4 even for billions of rows (see the storage engine note).

CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);

-- Uses the index: equality and range
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';
SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-08';

-- Does NOT use it (function hides the column)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'a@x.com';
-- Fix: expression index
CREATE INDEX users_email_lower_idx ON users (lower(email));

Selectivity matters. Selectivity = the fraction of rows a predicate matches. An index on status where 95 percent of rows are DONE is useless for status='DONE' but good for the rare status='FAILED' (see partial indexes below).

Decision gravity. Adding an index is a two-way door (you can drop it) but building one on a huge table is heavy I/O; use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres to avoid blocking writes. In MySQL, InnoDB online DDL covers most index builds.

Everyday analogy. A phone book sorted by name: easy to find "Sharma", easy to find all names between "Sa" and "Sh", useless to find everyone with a given phone number.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping an indexed column in a function or casting it (type mismatch like comparing a text column to an int).
  • Leading wildcard LIKE '%abc' cannot use a B-tree.
  • Forgetting ANALYZE; stale statistics lead to bad plans.

notes.title: Composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule
notes.html:
A composite (multi-column) index sorts by the first column, then the second within equal first values, and so on. So it helps queries that use a leftmost prefix of its columns.

CREATE INDEX orders_cust_status_created ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at);
Query Uses index well?
WHERE customer_id = 7 Yes (prefix)
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID' Yes
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID' ORDER BY created_at Yes, and no sort needed
WHERE status = 'PAID' Poor (skips first column; Postgres may use skip-style scan only in new versions, MySQL 8.0 has skip scan in limited cases)
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > ... Partly: uses customer_id, then filters on the rest

Column order rule of thumb (ESR-like): equality columns first, then sort columns, then range columns. Selectivity is a secondary tiebreaker, not the main rule.

Index on (customer_id, status, created_at) is sorted like:
 (1,'NEW','..'), (1,'PAID','..'), (1,'PAID','..'), (2,'NEW','..'), ...
Within customer 7 and PAID, rows are already sorted by created_at.

Worked example. Feed query: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Index (user_id, created_at DESC) reads exactly 20 index entries and stops. Index on user_id alone reads all of a user's 50,000 rows and sorts them.

Industry examples. MongoDB's compound index guidance (equality, sort, range), and Postgres/MySQL docs, give the same principle. Many "feed" and "inbox" tables at Slack-style apps use (owner_id, created_at).

Everyday analogy. A school register sorted by class, then by name: finding everyone in class 5 is easy; finding everyone named "Asha" in all classes is not.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating separate single-column indexes and expecting them to act like one composite (the planner may combine them with a bitmap AND, usually slower).
  • Redundant indexes: (a) is covered by (a, b); drop the smaller one.
  • Putting a range column before an equality column.

notes.title: Covering indexes and index-only scans
notes.html:
A covering index contains every column the query needs, so the database never touches the table. This avoids a random heap fetch per row.

-- Postgres: INCLUDE adds payload columns without making them part of the sort key
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_created_cov
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents, status);

SELECT created_at, total_cents, status
FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- EXPLAIN shows: Index Only Scan

In Postgres, index-only scans also require the visibility map to say the page is all-visible (kept fresh by VACUUM); otherwise it still visits the heap. MySQL InnoDB secondary indexes always carry the primary key, so a query needing only indexed columns plus the PK is covered ("Using index" in EXPLAIN).

Worked example. 20 rows via normal index = 1 index traversal + 20 random heap reads (could be 20 disk reads on a cold cache, about 2 ms on SSD). Covering = 1 traversal, all from the index, near 0.2 ms.

Trade-off. Wider index entries mean a bigger index, more RAM pressure and slower writes. Only cover your hottest queries.

Industry examples. InnoDB's clustered primary key and its secondary indexes storing the PK is the textbook case. DynamoDB's "projection" in a global secondary index is the same idea: choose KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE or ALL.

Everyday analogy. An index card that already lists the answer, so you never walk to the shelf.

Common interview traps.

  • SELECT * kills covering.
  • Forgetting VACUUM, so index-only scans quietly become normal scans.
  • Over-including columns and bloating the index.

notes.title: Partial and expression indexes
notes.html:
A partial index indexes only the rows matching a condition. Smaller index, cheaper writes, and a perfect fit for skewed data.

-- Only 2% of orders are pending, but the queue worker scans them constantly
CREATE INDEX orders_pending_idx ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Unique only among active rows (soft delete)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_active ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

The query must include a condition the planner can prove implies the index predicate (WHERE status='PENDING'). MySQL has no partial indexes (use generated columns or functional indexes).

Expression (functional) indexes index a computed value: CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)).

Worked example. 100M orders, 2 percent pending = 2M rows. Full index on created_at: about 2 GB. Partial: about 40 MB, which fits in cache, so the worker's poll query stays at sub-millisecond.

Industry examples. Soft-delete uniqueness and "job queue pending" indexes are standard in Postgres-heavy shops like GitLab and Stripe-style systems.

Everyday analogy. A sticky tab only on the pages marked "urgent", not on every page.

Common interview traps.

  • Query condition does not match the index predicate exactly, so the index is ignored.
  • Assuming MySQL supports partial indexes.

notes.title: Hash indexes
notes.html:
A hash index maps hash(key) to a bucket, giving O(1) equality lookups but no ordering. It cannot do range scans, sorting or prefix matches.

  • Postgres: hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe since version 10; occasionally smaller/faster than B-tree for equality on long keys, but B-tree is usually fine and more flexible.
  • MySQL InnoDB: has an internal adaptive hash index built automatically over hot B-tree pages; the MEMORY engine supports explicit hash indexes.
  • Distributed stores: hash partitioning of keys (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis Cluster) is the same idea, used to spread data across nodes.
CREATE INDEX sessions_token_hash ON sessions USING hash (token);
SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token = 'abc123';   -- uses hash
SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token > 'abc';      -- cannot use hash

Worked example. Looking up a 64-char session token: B-tree stores the whole key at every level (wide entries, lower fan-out); hash stores a 4-byte hash code, so the index is smaller. Gain is real but modest, which is why most teams stay with B-tree.

Decision gravity. Two-way door (just an index). But hash partitioning (sharding) is a one-way door: changing the hash or node count reshuffles data, which is why consistent hashing exists.

Industry examples. DynamoDB and Cassandra partition by hash of the partition key; Redis uses 16,384 hash slots.

Everyday analogy. A cloakroom numbered ticket: instant to find your coat, but impossible to ask for "all coats between ticket 100 and 200 in order of size".

Common interview traps.

  • Using hash for anything involving ranges or ORDER BY.
  • Confusing a hash index with hash partitioning.

notes.title: Inverted indexes and full-text search
notes.html:
An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it (a posting list). It is how search engines work, the reverse of the document-to-words view.

Build steps: tokenise text ("Fast red cars" to fast, red, car), normalise (lowercase, stem, remove stop words), store term -> sorted list of doc IDs (plus positions and frequencies). A query for red AND car intersects two sorted posting lists. Ranking uses TF-IDF or BM25.

doc1: "red fast car"      doc2: "red bike"     doc3: "fast car"
red  -> [1, 2]
fast -> [1, 3]
car  -> [1, 3]
bike -> [2]
Query "fast AND car" -> [1,3] ∩ [1,3] = [1,3]
-- Postgres full-text and GIN
CREATE INDEX docs_fts ON docs USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body));
SELECT id FROM docs WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('fast & car');

Postgres GIN (Generalised Inverted Index) also indexes JSONB keys and array elements: CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops). Lucene (inside Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr) writes immutable segments merged in the background (an LSM-like pattern).

Worked example. 100M product descriptions averaging 50 words. Scanning with LIKE '%shoe%' is hopeless (seconds to minutes). An inverted index finds the posting list for shoe and returns results in tens of milliseconds, including ranking.

Operational notes. Elasticsearch is near-real-time: new docs become searchable after a refresh (default 1 s). It is a derived index fed from the source of truth via CDC; do not use it as the only copy of data.

Industry examples. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch power search at Uber, Netflix, Wikipedia; Lucene underneath. Postgres FTS suffices for small to medium workloads. Google's web index is a giant sharded inverted index.

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a book: from a word straight to the pages, not the other way round.

Common interview traps.

  • Using LIKE '%term%' on a big table.
  • Treating Elasticsearch as a primary database.
  • Forgetting the analyzer: a query analysed differently from the index will miss matches.

notes.title: Geo and spatial indexes
notes.html:
A geo index answers "what is near this point" or "what is inside this area" quickly. A plain B-tree on (lat, lng) is bad because two-dimensional nearness does not map to one-dimensional sort order.

Main approaches:

  • R-tree (and GiST in Postgres/PostGIS): a tree of bounding rectangles; query prunes rectangles that do not overlap.
  • Geohash: encode lat/lng into a base-32 string where a common prefix means nearby (6 chars is about 1.2 km x 0.6 km, 7 chars about 150 m). Stored in any B-tree or key-value store; query the cell plus its 8 neighbours.
  • Quadtree: recursively split a square into four.
  • S2 (Google) and H3 (Uber): map the sphere to cells with hierarchy; H3 uses hexagons so all neighbours are equidistant.
-- PostGIS
CREATE INDEX places_geo ON places USING gist (location);
SELECT name FROM places
WHERE ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint(73.85, 18.52)::geography, 2000)  -- 2 km
ORDER BY location <-> ST_MakePoint(73.85, 18.52)::geography LIMIT 10;

Edge-case warning (geohash): two points can be very close but sit on opposite sides of a cell boundary with different prefixes. Always query neighbouring cells, then compute exact distance.

Worked example. 5M drivers, each updating every 4 s = 1.25M location writes/s globally. Storing the live position in Redis (GEOADD, backed by a sorted set with geohash scores) handles hot ephemeral data; durable history goes to a different store. Uber uses H3 for supply/demand and pricing zones.

Industry examples. Uber (H3), Google Maps (S2), Lyft, Foursquare, Redis GEOSEARCH, MongoDB 2dsphere, Elasticsearch geo_point, PostGIS GiST.

Everyday analogy. Dividing a city into labelled grid squares on a map: to find nearby cafes you look in your square and the eight around it.

Common interview traps.

  • Using two B-trees (lat and lng) and intersecting; extremely slow.
  • Ignoring the cell-boundary problem.
  • Ignoring that the poles and the date line distort naive grids.

notes.title: How to pick an index, and how to verify
notes.html:
Work backwards from the query. Process:

  1. List the top queries with QPS and latency target.
  2. For each, note equality filters, range filters, sort and returned columns.
  3. Choose the type: equality+range+sort = B-tree (composite); equality only on long keys = hash; skewed subset = partial; text = inverted; location = geo; JSON/array containment = GIN.
  4. Add INCLUDE columns only for the hottest paths.
  5. Verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in Postgres or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in MySQL. Look for Seq Scan on big tables, large Rows Removed by Filter, Sort nodes where an index could provide order, and estimated rows far from actual.
  6. Remove unused indexes: pg_stat_user_indexes (idx_scan = 0).
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Workload Index
WHERE a=? AND b=? ORDER BY c B-tree (a, b, c)
Session token equality B-tree or hash
Queue of pending rows Partial on status
Search box Inverted (GIN / Elasticsearch)
Nearby places GiST / geohash / H3
JSON field filtering GIN on JSONB

Incident pattern. Symptom: CPU high and p99 up after a deploy that changed a query. Metric: pg_stat_statements shows a query with huge shared_blks_read and a Seq Scan in EXPLAIN. Fix: add or correct an index with CONCURRENTLY.

Industry examples. Postgres teams use pg_stat_statements and auto_explain; MySQL teams use the slow query log with pt-query-digest.

Everyday analogy. A mechanic does not guess; they plug in a diagnostic reader (EXPLAIN) before replacing parts.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding indexes without measuring before and after.
  • Not saying what you would index for writes-heavy tables (fewer indexes).
  • Forgetting indexes in distributed stores: Cassandra secondary indexes on high-cardinality columns are discouraged; model a new table instead.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An index speeds reads by trading write cost, disk and RAM; the planner may still skip it.
  • B-tree is the default: equality, range, sort, prefix. No functions on indexed columns without expression indexes.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality columns, then sort, then range.
  • Covering indexes (INCLUDE, InnoDB PK trick) avoid table fetches; they need VACUUM in Postgres and avoid SELECT *.
  • Partial indexes shrink indexes for skewed data (pending rows, active rows); not in MySQL.
  • Hash indexes: equality only. Inverted indexes: text search via posting lists. Geo indexes: R-tree/GiST, geohash, S2, H3 with neighbour-cell checks.
  • Pick from the query shape, verify with EXPLAIN, remove unused indexes, build with CONCURRENTLY.

questions.promptHtml: What does an index buy you and what does it cost? Why not index every column?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates "indexes make it fast" from understanding the write, memory and planner trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An index lets the database seek to rows instead of scanning the table, turning tens of seconds into about a millisecond on a 100M-row table. The cost: every insert, delete and update of an indexed column must also update each index, and each index takes disk and RAM. So I index for the queries that matter and drop the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: orders, 100M rows x 200 B = 20 GB. An index on customer_id is about 20 B per entry, so about 2 GB. With 5 indexes one insert modifies the table page plus 5 index pages: about 6 page modifications and 6 WAL records, so write throughput falls as indexes pile up. Indexes compete for the buffer cache with the table itself.

The planner may ignore an index: if the predicate matches a large fraction of rows (say over 5 to 10 percent, depends on cost model) a sequential scan is cheaper than many random fetches. Low-selectivity columns such as booleans rarely benefit from a plain index.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Add an index" without checking write cost and memory.
  • Indexing a boolean or a column with 3 distinct values.
  • Leaving unused indexes in place for years.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How find unused indexes? -> Postgres pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan = 0 over a long enough window.
  2. Which writes pay for an index? -> Inserts, deletes, and updates to the indexed columns (Postgres HOT updates can skip index changes when no indexed column changes).
  3. Why might the planner skip a valid index? -> Low selectivity, stale statistics, or a function or cast on the column.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "indexes speed reads and slow writes". The senior quantifies size and write amplification, mentions selectivity and the buffer cache, and ties each index to a named query.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A table with 14 indexes was the main bottleneck for bulk loads; dropping 6 unused ones cut insert time by about a third.

questions.promptHtml: You have WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at. How do you order the columns in a composite index and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Column order is the most common indexing mistake, and the answer shows if you understand how a composite index is sorted.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A composite index sorts by the first column, then the second within equal first values, and so on. So it helps queries that use a leftmost prefix. My rule is equality columns first, then the sort column, then range columns: (customer_id, status, created_at). Selectivity is only a tiebreaker.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Index (customer_id, status, created_at) is sorted like:
 (1,'NEW','..'), (1,'PAID','..'), (1,'PAID','..'), (2,'NEW','..'), ...
Within customer 7 and PAID, rows are already ordered by created_at.

Seek to customer 7, then status PAID, then scan the created_at range in order: no sort node and only the slice is read. If the range column were first, the engine would scan a big range and filter on the rest.

Query Uses index well?
WHERE customer_id = 7 yes (prefix)
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status='PAID' yes
WHERE status='PAID' poor; skips the first column (skip scan exists only in some engines/versions, verify)
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > ... partly: uses customer_id, filters the rest 
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_status_created ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Range column before equality column.
  • Expecting two single-column indexes to behave like one composite (a bitmap AND is usually slower).
  • Keeping redundant (a) next to (a, b).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the query only filters on status? -> It needs its own index (or a partial one); the composite cannot seek on a non-leading column.
  2. How does ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT 20 benefit? -> (user_id, created_at DESC) reads 20 entries and stops instead of sorting 50,000.
  3. Where does selectivity matter? -> Among several equality columns, put the more selective one first only when no other rule decides it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "most selective column first". The senior uses the equality, sort, range rule, checks the plan for a Sort node, and drops redundant indexes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed query sorting 50,000 rows per request dropped from 120 ms to 2 ms after the index got created_at as its second column.

questions.contextHtml:
A login endpoint is slow after a deploy, p99 jumped from 5 ms to 900 ms. The users table has 40M rows and an index on email. The new code:

SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower($1);

and a second endpoint:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;   -- phone is varchar(15), indexed

EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan on users for both. A teammate says "the index is corrupted, rebuild it".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with each query and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rebuilds the index or adds a second plain index on the same column. It does not notice that the predicate hides the column.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are emails stored mixed-case? Can I change the query? Do we need case-insensitive uniqueness? Which Postgres or MySQL version (collation, citext, generated column options differ)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the deploy if possible, or create the expression index concurrently on the live table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lower(email) on the column prevents a plain B-tree on email from being used. (b) phone = 9876543210 compares varchar to a number, causing an implicit cast on the column. (c) Stale statistics. (d) Index corruption (unlikely).
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on both and look for Seq Scan and Filter: with a cast; run \d users to see index definitions; check pg_stat_user_tables for last analyze.
  5. Root cause: An index is sorted by the raw column value. Wrapping the column in a function or implicit cast produces a value the index does not contain, so the planner must evaluate it per row.
  6. Fix:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_lower_idx ON users (lower(email));
-- phone: pass a string, not a number
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';

For uniqueness use CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... (lower(email)), or normalise email to lowercase at write time and keep the plain index. 7. Prevention: Run EXPLAIN on new queries in review, use typed parameters, and alert on seq scans from pg_stat_statements. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The expression index adds a write cost, so if I can normalise at write time I prefer that. Do not rebuild a healthy index. CONCURRENTLY takes longer and can leave an invalid index on failure, so check afterwards.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• LIKE '%gmail.com'? -> A leading wildcard cannot use a B-tree; use a reversed-string expression index or trigram (pg_trgm) index.
  • Do ORMs cause this? -> Yes, through implicit casts and wrapping functions; log real SQL.
  • MySQL equivalent? -> Functional indexes (8.0.13+) or a generated column; verify version.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" lower() added in a refactor moved a login path from index seek to scanning 40M rows and tripled CPU at peak.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rebuilds the index.
  • Hire: spots the function and the cast, adds an expression index or fixes the type.
  • Strong hire: uses CONCURRENTLY, considers write-time normalisation and builds a review/monitoring guard.

questions.contextHtml:
A notifications table has 500M rows. The hot query serves 3,000 QPS:

SELECT id, type, created_at FROM notifications
WHERE user_id = $1 AND read = false
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Current index: (user_id). A typical user has 4,000 notifications, 3 percent unread. p99 is 60 ms; EXPLAIN shows Sort and Rows Removed by Filter: 3880.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index on read" (boolean, low selectivity) or on every column separately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the unread count also needed (separate query)? Does read flip often (index churn)? Is there a retention policy? What is the write rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; create the new index concurrently.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Reading all 4,000 rows then filtering and sorting is the cost. (b) A composite (user_id, read, created_at DESC) serves it with no sort. (c) A partial index on unread rows is even smaller.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for each candidate; check the index size and write cost.
  5. Root cause: The existing index finds the user's rows but cannot filter on read or return them in order, so we fetch about 4,000 heap rows, discard 97 percent and sort.
  6. Fix:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY notif_unread_idx
  ON notifications (user_id, created_at DESC) WHERE read = false;

Only 3 percent of rows (about 15M entries) are indexed, the entries are already sorted by time, and the query reads 20 entries and stops. 7. Prevention: Include the unread query in the performance test set; watch index size and bloat as rows flip from unread to read (each flip removes an entry). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Partial index means other queries (read items) need another plan. The flip read=true is an index delete plus possibly a non-HOT update, so heavy flipping adds churn; MySQL has no partial indexes, so there I would use (user_id, read, created_at).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need "all notifications" feed too? -> A second index (user_id, created_at DESC).
  • Mark-all-read touches 4,000 rows? -> Batch it and watch bloat.
  • Why not covering? -> Add INCLUDE (type, id) only if heap fetches show up as the bottleneck.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Swapping a full composite for a partial unread index shrank it from 30 GB to about 1 GB, which kept it in RAM and held p99 at about 2 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single-column index on read.
  • Hire: composite with equality then sort column.
  • Strong hire: partial index with size math, notes the MySQL alternative and the write churn.

questions.subtopic: Partial index for a job queue
questions.contextHtml:
A jobs table has 100M rows, of which about 2 percent are status = 'PENDING'. Workers poll constantly:

SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100;

The full index on (status, created_at) is 3.4 GB, and index maintenance on completed jobs is hot. A second requirement: usernames must be unique among non-deleted users (deleted_at IS NULL) but a deleted user's name can be reused.
questions.promptHtml: What indexes would you create, and what are the pitfalls?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps the full index and adds a unique constraint on username, which breaks name reuse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do statuses change often? Are there multiple workers (needs SKIP LOCKED)? Which database? MySQL has no partial indexes.
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is an optimisation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A partial index on pending rows is about 2 percent of the size. (b) Query predicate must match the index predicate exactly. (c) Unique partial index solves the reuse rule.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN must show the partial index; compare pg_relation_size.
  5. Root cause: Most rows are DONE, so indexing them is wasted memory and write work.
  6. Fix:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_pending_idx ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_username_active ON users (username) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

Estimated 2M entries, about 70 MB, fits in cache. Query must say WHERE status = 'PENDING' literally; a bound parameter status = $1 may not be provable, so use the literal (verify with your driver and generic plans). 7. Prevention: Test the plan with the app's real query form; add a test asserting EXPLAIN uses the index. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A row leaving PENDING removes its index entry, fine. I would not use a partial index on a column whose predicate changes meaning later. For many workers use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so they do not block each other.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• On MySQL? -> No partial indexes; use a separate pending table or a generated column and a regular index.
  • Status values grow (RETRY, FAILED)? -> Adjust the predicate to IN (...) and rebuild.
  • Why not hash index? -> Poll needs ordering by created_at; hash gives equality only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue index shrank from 3 GB to 60 MB with a partial index and the poll query dropped from 6 ms to 0.3 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: full index on status.
  • Hire: partial index with matching predicate and the unique soft-delete variant.
  • Strong hire: size math, parameter-matching pitfall, SKIP LOCKED and the MySQL alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
After a Tuesday deploy, a Postgres primary (16 vCPU, 128 GB RAM) goes from 30 percent to 95 percent CPU, p99 API latency 40 ms to 3 s. Deploy touched a reporting endpoint. pg_stat_statements top entry:

query: SELECT ... FROM events WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2 AND type = ANY($3) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50
calls: 9,200/min   mean_exec_time: 1,850 ms   shared_blks_read: 42,000,000
Limit  -> Sort -> Seq Scan on events (rows=412M)  Filter: (tenant_id = ..)  Rows Removed by Filter: 411,998,000

Existing index: (created_at). Table is 380 GB, taking 8,000 writes/s. The team wants to add (tenant_id), (type), and (created_at, tenant_id) indexes to be safe.
questions.promptHtml: Handle the incident and design the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Creates three indexes at once, non-concurrently, on a 380 GB table at peak: it blocks writes and may make things worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which deploy changed the query (was it indexed before)? How selective is tenant_id (skew: one big tenant)? Can we roll back? Free disk and I/O headroom for an index build?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back or disable the reporting endpoint, add a rate limit and a statement timeout. That stops the bleeding without touching the table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) New query shape has no matching index, so a Seq Scan. (b) Stale statistics pushed the planner away from (created_at). (c) A large tenant makes the existing index scan plus filter expensive. (d) Parameter type mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with a real parameter set, pg_stat_user_tables for last analyze, row distribution per tenant, auto_explain for generic vs custom plans.
  5. Root cause: Query has equality on tenant_id and type, a range plus sort on created_at. No index leads with tenant_id, so the engine reads 412M rows.
  6. Fix: One index built concurrently, off-peak, with I/O throttled:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_tenant_created_idx ON events (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

type = ANY(...) can be filtered cheaply because the first rows come back already sorted and LIMIT 50 stops early; add type only if EXPLAIN shows many filtered rows. Check size: about 412M x about 30 B = about 12 GB; verify free space and replication lag. 7. Prevention: Run EXPLAIN on new queries in CI against production-like data, alert on Seq Scan over big tables, and use pg_stat_statements diffs after every deploy. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Three speculative indexes triple write cost at 8,000 writes/s. Non-concurrent builds block writes for minutes to hours. After deploy, drop (created_at) only if pg_stat_user_indexes shows it unused.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Build fails halfway? -> Leaves an INVALID index; drop and retry.
  • Replica lag climbs during the build? -> Throttle with maintenance settings or build in a quieter window.
  • One tenant has 60 percent of rows? -> Partial or per-tenant strategy, or partitioning by tenant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single concurrent index restored a primary from 95 percent CPU in 25 minutes; the earlier "index everything" attempt had stalled writes for 10.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blindly adds indexes.
  • Hire: mitigates first, finds the query via pg_stat_statements, one correct composite index with CONCURRENTLY.
  • Strong hire: sizing, replica lag, skew handling, rollback plan and a CI guard.

questions.promptHtml: What is a covering index? Why might an index-only scan in Postgres still hit the table?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks understanding of heap fetches and the Postgres visibility map, which is a common gap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A covering index holds every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index without fetching table rows. In Postgres I add payload columns with INCLUDE. An index-only scan still visits the heap for pages the visibility map does not mark all-visible, so stale VACUUM makes it quietly degrade.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_created_cov
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents, status);

SELECT created_at, total_cents, status FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;   -- Index Only Scan

A normal index does one traversal plus 20 random heap reads (maybe 2 ms on SSD, more on a cold cache). Covering does one traversal, about 0.2 ms. The visibility rule: an index entry does not store transaction visibility, so Postgres checks the visibility map; if the page is not all-visible it fetches the heap tuple. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows Heap Fetches: N. In InnoDB the secondary index entries carry the primary key, so a query needing only indexed columns plus the PK is covered (Using index).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• SELECT * defeats covering.
  • Forgetting vacuum on a write-heavy table, so Heap Fetches stays high.
  • Including many wide columns and bloating the index.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between key columns and INCLUDE columns? -> Key columns are sorted and searchable; INCLUDE columns are only payload and do not affect order.
  2. Trade-off? -> Larger index, more RAM and slower writes; cover only the hottest queries.
  3. DynamoDB analogue? -> Global secondary index projection: KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE or ALL.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "no table lookup". The senior explains the visibility map, checks Heap Fetches in the plan, and weighs index size and write cost before including columns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard query had an index-only plan on paper but 90 percent heap fetches because autovacuum lagged on a hot table.

questions.promptHtml: How does an inverted index work, and when would you use Postgres full-text search versus Elasticsearch?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Search is a common feature; seniors must explain the mechanism and the operational consequences of a derived index.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted posting list of document IDs. Text is analysed (tokenised, lowercased, stemmed) at index time and again at query time; a AND b intersects two posting lists, and results are ranked with TF-IDF or BM25. Postgres FTS with a GIN index is enough for small to medium workloads; Elasticsearch is for large corpora, faceting and relevance tuning, but it is a derived store fed from the source of truth, near real time, not a primary database.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
doc1 "red fast car"   doc2 "red bike"   doc3 "fast car"
red -> [1,2]   fast -> [1,3]   car -> [1,3]   bike -> [2]
"fast AND car" -> [1,3] intersect [1,3] = [1,3]
CREATE INDEX docs_fts ON docs USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body));
SELECT id FROM docs WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('fast & car');

Lucene (under Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr) writes immutable segments merged in the background, an LSM-like pattern. New documents become searchable after a refresh (default 1 s). Index it via CDC or an outbox; build with an alias so you can reindex without downtime.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• LIKE '%term%' on a big table.
  • Analyzer mismatch between index and query, causing missed matches.
  • Treating Elasticsearch as the only copy of data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep it in sync? -> CDC (e.g. Debezium) or transactional outbox, with idempotent upserts and a reindex path.
  2. What if search results lag by minutes? -> Check refresh interval, bulk queue lag and CDC lag.
  3. Typo tolerance? -> Fuzzy queries or n-gram analyzers; costs index size.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "use Elasticsearch for search". The senior sizes whether Postgres is enough, explains the analyzer and posting lists, and treats the search index as rebuildable derived data with a sync strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team lost searchable data after a cluster failure because Elasticsearch was the only copy; they added CDC from the database as the source of truth.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing service has 5 million drivers, each reporting location every 4 s (1.25M writes/s globally). A rider request needs "the 10 nearest available drivers within 2 km", under 50 ms. The first design stores lat and lng in Postgres with two B-tree indexes and queries lat BETWEEN ... AND lng BETWEEN .... At 5,000 requests/s the DB falls over. A geohash cell prototype works but support tickets say drivers just across a street are missed.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how would you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more read replicas". It ignores that 2-D proximity does not map onto two 1-D B-trees and that live positions are an ephemeral, high-write dataset.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the location durable or only latest-position? Per-city or global search? How fresh must positions be? Do we also need history for pricing and safety?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a short per-city cache and cap search radius while the redesign lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Two B-tree range scans intersected return huge candidate sets (a long thin strip each). (b) 1.25M writes/s against a durable relational store is wasted work. (c) Geohash boundary bug: neighbours not searched.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN shows bitmap AND on two indexes; check write amplification; reproduce the missed-driver case on a cell boundary.
  5. Root cause: Nearness in 2-D is not preserved by sorting on one coordinate, and a point right next to a cell edge has a different geohash prefix.
  6. Fix: Keep live positions in an in-memory geo structure (e.g. Redis GEOADD/GEOSEARCH, a sorted set with geohash scores) sharded by city or cell, with TTL on stale drivers. Query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours, then compute exact distance and sort. Durable history goes to a different store. For analytics zones, H3 hexagons give equidistant neighbours.
  7. Prevention: Test boundary cases and the date line and poles; load test at 2x peak.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cell size is a trade: 6-char geohash is about 1.2 km x 0.6 km, so a 2 km search touches several cells; finer cells mean more lookups. Do not write every ping to Postgres/PostGIS at 1.25M/s; use PostGIS GiST only for the durable, lower-rate data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dense downtown cell with 10,000 drivers? -> Use a finer cell resolution or adaptive quadtree.
  • Redis node dies? -> Positions repopulate in seconds from the next pings; no durability needed.
  • Why H3 over geohash? -> Hex cells have uniform neighbour distance; geohash rectangles distort with latitude.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A matching service dropped from 800 ms to 20 ms moving to a cell-based in-memory index, and a one-line fix to search all 9 cells cured the missing-driver tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: two B-tree indexes or replicas.
  • Hire: geohash or R-tree with neighbour cells and exact-distance filter.
  • Strong hire: separates ephemeral from durable data, does write-rate math, and handles boundary and density issues.

questions.contextHtml:
A Postgres payments table (900M rows, 700 GB data) has 14 indexes totalling 1.1 TB. Insert rate is 6,000 rows/s at peak with p99 insert latency 120 ms (target 20 ms). Replica lag spikes to 40 s during peaks. Autovacuum runs constantly. The DBA's stats:

indexrelname           idx_scan   size
pay_user_idx           8,900,000  64 GB
pay_user_created_idx   0          91 GB
pay_status_idx         12         48 GB
pay_created_idx        210,000    52 GB
pay_merchant_idx       5,300,000  71 GB
... (9 more, 6 with idx_scan < 100)

The stats were last reset 11 days ago. A lead says "drop all with low scans today".
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide what to drop and how do you do it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Drops everything with low scans immediately, missing monthly reports, unique constraints, replicas and the short stats window.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do any low-scan indexes back unique or FK constraints? Are there month-end or quarter-end jobs? Do reads go to replicas (stats are per node)? Is stats reset recent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing destructive; collect more evidence. Throttle non-essential writers if lag is dangerous.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Several indexes are unused or redundant (pay_user_created_idx is a superset of pay_user_idx: the opposite may be needed). (b) Write amplification from 14 indexes drives latency, WAL volume and replica lag. (c) Bloat from index churn.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pull pg_stat_user_indexes from primary and replicas over a full business cycle (at least one month-end), cross-check with pg_stat_statements, and check constraints with pg_index.indisunique and FK needs. Measure WAL bytes per insert.
  5. Root cause: Each insert touches the table plus 14 indexes: about 15 page changes and WAL records, so insert cost scales with index count. Unused indexes are pure cost.
  6. Fix: Build a drop list with evidence: look at redundancy first: pay_user_idx (8.9M scans) is a prefix of pay_user_created_idx (0 scans), so one of them is dead weight. Find out why the planner never picks the wider one (queries without ORDER BY created_at?) before choosing which to drop. For each candidate: hide first by confirming no plan uses it (e.g. run in a staging copy or check with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY plus a recorded CREATE script for rollback). Drop one or two per day and watch latency and slow query logs.
  7. Prevention: Index review in PRs, a quarterly unused-index report, and a rule that each index names the query it serves.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dropping an index is cheap to undo in code but a rebuild on 70 GB takes hours and I/O. I would not drop unique/PK-backing indexes, nor decide from an 11-day window. Expected win: removing 6 indexes cuts per-insert page writes from about 15 to about 9.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A month-end report breaks after the drop? -> Rebuild concurrently from the saved definition; that is why we keep it.
  • Replica serves reports? -> Gather stats there too; they are not shared.
  • Can we avoid the index cost for historical rows? -> Partition by time and keep indexes on hot partitions only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Removing 7 indexes with zero scans over 60 days cut peak insert p99 from 110 ms to 25 ms and replica lag from 40 s to 3 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: drops by gut or by one query.
  • Hire: uses idx_scan over a long window, checks constraints and replicas.
  • Strong hire: staged drops with rollback scripts, WAL math, partitioning option and review process.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks for "a search box on our catalogue". 8 million products, descriptions of about 50 words, 300 queries/s at peak, 50 new or changed products per second. Today the app uses WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' and takes 4 s. Engineering is debating Postgres full-text search versus a new Elasticsearch cluster.
questions.promptHtml: How would you decide, and what are the risks of the option you pick?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Elasticsearch, it is made for search" with no sizing, sync plan or failure modes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does good search mean: typo tolerance, synonyms, facets, ranking by popularity? How fresh must results be (seconds, minutes)? Which languages? Who operates a new cluster? What is the latency SLO?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quick win now: stop leading-wildcard scans with a pg_trgm GIN index, which makes ILIKE '%term%' indexable (verify extension availability).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 8M rows x 50 words fits Postgres FTS with GIN comfortably at 300 QPS. (b) Facets, fuzzy matching and relevance tuning favour Elasticsearch/OpenSearch. (c) The unknown requirement decides.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype Postgres FTS (tsvector generated column with GIN) and measure p99 at 2x load; list required features against what each tool does.
  5. Root cause: The slowness is just a missing inverted index; the real question is feature scope.
  6. Fix: If requirements are basic: Postgres tsvector + GIN, ranked with ts_rank; no new system. If faceting, typo tolerance and relevance tuning are required: Elasticsearch fed by CDC from Postgres, with the DB staying the source of truth, writes idempotent upserts by product ID, and a reindex-by-alias procedure.
  7. Prevention: Monitor sync lag (CDC lag, refresh time), search p99, and error rate; keep a rebuild runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Elasticsearch adds a cluster to run, near-real-time lag (default refresh 1 s) and dual-write risk. I would not write to both stores from the app without an outbox. The first choice is reversible if search stays behind an interface.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product changes must appear instantly? -> Query the DB by ID for the edited item, or accept refresh delay.
  • Analyzer change needs reindex? -> Yes; build a new index, switch alias.
  • Elasticsearch down? -> Degrade to basic Postgres search or cached results.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team ran Elasticsearch for 100k products when Postgres FTS would do; another trusted it as the primary store and lost data in a bad upgrade.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tool choice without questions.
  • Hire: clarifies requirements, proposes inverted index with the right size reasoning.
  • Strong hire: phased plan, sync via CDC/outbox, rebuild path and degrade mode.

questions.subtopic: Changing an index under live traffic
questions.contextHtml: A MySQL 8 InnoDB table events has 2 billion rows (900 GB) and takes 12,000 writes/s. The current index (user_id) is too weak: the hot query filters by user_id and type and sorts by created_at. Plan: replace it with (user_id, type, created_at). Last quarter a plain ALTER TABLE ... ADD INDEX on a smaller table caused 20 minutes of replica lag and a spike in deadlocks. There is a 99.95 percent availability SLO.
questions.promptHtml: How do you ship the new index with no outage, and how do you retire the old one?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the ALTER at night." Ignores replica lag, metadata locks and rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the table have replicas that serve reads? Free disk for a 100+ GB index? Longest running transaction? Do we have an online schema-change tool (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; the plan is risk containment.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) metadata lock stalls from long transactions at the start and end of DDL. (b) Replica lag when the DDL replays on replicas. (c) Disk and I/O saturation. (d) Plan flips on query after the change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test the DDL on a clone sized like production and time it; check performance_schema metadata locks and long transactions before starting; estimate index size: 2B rows x about 40 B = about 80 GB plus overhead.
  5. Root cause: Index builds are heavy I/O and DDL needs brief metadata locks; replicas apply them serially, so lag is the main risk.
  6. Fix: Use InnoDB online DDL (ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE) or gh-ost, throttled on replica lag and load, with a checked disk budget. Add the new index first, keep the old one. Compare EXPLAIN and slow-log metrics on the new plan via canary traffic or FORCE INDEX in a test. Only after a week of stable metrics drop (user_id), since (user_id, type, created_at) covers its prefix. Keep the DDL script for rollback.
  7. Prevention: A runbook for large DDL, pre-checks for long transactions, lag-based throttling and index review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dropping the old index right away removes the fallback; it is cheap to recreate only in time, not in hours. Never run big DDL on the primary with a transaction open for hours; it blocks. gh-ost copies the table, so it needs about double disk; verify against the in-place option.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Replica lag hits 60 s? -> Throttle or pause the change, which both tools support.
  • DDL fails halfway? -> In-place DDL rolls back; a gh-ost run can be aborted with the original table untouched.
  • Postgres equivalent? -> CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A throttled online index build over two days caused no user impact, while an earlier "quick" ALTER at midnight produced a 20-minute lag and a rollback.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: direct ALTER at night.
  • Hire: online DDL with replica-lag awareness and keep old index until verified.
  • Strong hire: sizing, metadata-lock checks, canary validation, rollback and retire plan.
